blocks.title: What ICAI's published papers tell us
bullets: ICAI has published no examiners' comments for Paper 6; the guidance below comes from its suggested answers, RTPs and MTPs.

**This chapter is asked in every attempt, and it is the cheapest chapter in the paper to score in.** Nine past-paper parts between May 2024 and May 2026, a question in every one of the eight RTPs, and a question in thirteen of the MTPs — against only sixteen SM headings and three formulae.

**Three formulae carry almost every mark.** Walter's P = [D + (r ÷ Ke)(E − D)] ÷ Ke; Gordon's P₀ = E₁(1 − b) ÷ (Ke − br); and MM's P₀ = (P₁ + D₁) ÷ (1 + Ke). Learn them cold and the chapter is arithmetic.

**The commonest single step is finding EPS before anything else.** Net profit, less preference dividend, divided by the number of shares. Gamma Ltd, K Ltd, QB Ltd, Saraswati Ltd and the RTP Walter questions all begin there, and a wrong EPS makes every later figure wrong.

**The 2-mark and 4-mark theory slots rotate through a short list**: the assumptions of MM, the assumptions of Gordon, the limitations of Walter, the parameters of Lintner's Model, the forms of dividend, and the advantages and limitations of stock splits — asked eight times across the past papers and MTPs.

blocks.title: How ICAI marks this chapter (study guidance)
bullets: **Write the EPS working as a labelled statement**, even when the question looks like it only wants a price. Net profit − preference dividend = earnings for equity shareholders ÷ number of shares = EPS.

**Compare r with Ke and say so in words.** 'Since r of 25% exceeds Ke of 20%, the optimum payout is zero, so the company's 40% payout is not optimal' is the sentence that earns the comment mark in every Walter question.
**Under MM, prove the value is unchanged.** Compute the value both ways and state that they are equal; the mark is for the conclusion that dividend policy is irrelevant, not for the two numbers.

**Watch the reverse workings.** Four official questions give the price and ask for the dividend, the payout ratio, the retention ratio or r — so be able to run every formula backwards as well as forwards.
Where a question gives a **P/E ratio**, remember that Ke = 1 ÷ (P/E). Three RTP and MTP questions turn on that single substitution.

concepts.title: 1–2 Dividend Decisions and the Meaning of Dividend
understand: ==Long-term finance function decisions broadly cover three areas: **financing decision, investment decision and dividend decision**. Financing was Chapters 4 to 6 and investment was Chapter 7; this chapter is the third.==

==**ICAI's own framing of the difficulty: 'Dividend Decision is easy to understand but difficult to implement.'**== Suppose X Limited, which has been paying dividend at a normal growth rate, earns huge profits this year. If management pays a **higher** dividend, next year's growth may not support it and the dividend would have to fall. If management **stays** on the normal rate, the surplus retained earnings remain idle — ==**which will result in over capitalization if no other opportunity exists to utilise the idle funds**==.

==**Meaning of dividend** (SM §2): **dividend is that part of Profit After Tax (PAT) which is distributed to the shareholders of the company**. Profit earned after paying taxes can be used for **(i) distribution of dividend, or (ii) retaining as surplus for future growth**.==

==**Ex-dividend.** ==**Ex-dividend refers to shares that no longer carry the right to dividend. The price at which shares trade immediately on the next day after declaration of dividend is referred to as the ex-dividend price.**== The practical consequence is that when a dividend of ₹50 is declared on a share quoted at ₹200, the share trades at ₹150 the next day — the shareholder's wealth has not changed, only its form.

==**The two families of theory** (SM §1), which the whole chapter is organised around:
**Irrelevance Theory: MM Approach**
**Relevance Theory: Walter's Model, Gordon's Model and Lintner Model**==

One point of SM housekeeping worth knowing before you start. The chapter-overview diagram lists **four** theories including Lintner, but the body places **Lintner's Model inside §7 (Practical Considerations in Dividend Policy)** under payout policies, and the diagram at §8.1 shows only **MM, Walter and Gordon**. The register follows the body, so Lintner is §7 material — see F08.07.
concepts.example: A company that has always paid ₹5 a share earns an exceptional profit. Paying ₹8 this year risks a visible cut next year; paying ₹5 and finding no use for the surplus risks over-capitalisation. Nothing in the arithmetic of the chapter resolves that; what the models do is tell you which choice the share price should reward.

mcqs.question: The ex-dividend price of a share is:

options.A: The price at which the share trades immediately on the next day after declaration of dividend
options.B: The price at which the share traded on the day the dividend was recommended by the Board
options.C: The face value of the share increased by the dividend declared
options.D: The price at which the company will buy the share back

mcqs.explanation: SM §2: ex-dividend refers to shares that no longer carry the right to dividend, and the price at which shares trade immediately on the next day after declaration of dividend is referred to as the ex-dividend price.

why_wrong.B: That is the cum-dividend price — the share still carries the right then.
why_wrong.C: Face value plays no part in the definition.
why_wrong.D: That is a buyback or tender price, dealt with in §10.

mcqs.trap: The word 'ex' means the right has gone, so the price falls by roughly the dividend.

mcqs.question: The study material warns that if a company stays on its normal rate of dividend and has no opportunity to use the surplus retained earnings, the result will be:

options.A: Over-trading
options.B: Over-capitalization
options.C: A fall in the market price to the ex-dividend level
options.D: A breach of Section 123 of the Companies Act, 2013

mcqs.explanation: SM §1: if the company decides to stay on the normal rate of dividend, the surplus amount of retained earnings would remain idle, which will result in over capitalization if no other opportunity exists to utilise the idle funds.

why_wrong.A: Over-trading is too much business on too little capital — the opposite problem.
why_wrong.C: The ex-dividend fall happens whenever a dividend is declared and is not a consequence of retention.
why_wrong.D: Section 123 governs the source of dividend, not the decision to retain.

mcqs.trap: Idle capital, not insufficient capital, is the risk ICAI names here.

recap: Dividend is the part of profit after tax distributed to shareholders; the alternative is retention for future growth.
Ex-dividend shares no longer carry the right to dividend; the ex-dividend price is the next day's price after declaration.
Paying too much risks a visible cut next year; paying too little risks over-capitalisation.
Irrelevance theory is MM; relevance theory is Walter, Gordon and Lintner.

concepts.title: 3 Forms of Dividend
concepts.evidence: PYQ 0 · RTP 0 · MTP 2 (Jan 2025 Series II, Jan 2026 Series II)
understand: ==**Three forms** (SM §3): **1. Cash dividend** — the most common form. ==**Cash here means cash, cheque, warrant, demand draft, pay order or directly through Electronic Clearing Service (ECS) but not in kind.**==

==**2. Share repurchases** — a transaction in which the company buys back its own shares using corporate cash. The bought back shares can be classified as ==**(a) treasury shares, kept for re-issuance in future, or (b) cancelled shares, if they are retired from issued share capital**==. ==**Share repurchases are also viewed as one form of dividend distribution**, and keeping other things the same, **the effect of cash dividend and share repurchases on shareholders' wealth is the same**.==

**The equivalence worked, because ICAI prints it and an MCQ can be built on it.** HM Ltd has 1 crore equity shares and proposes a dividend of ₹50 a share — ₹50 crores in all. Market price is ₹200 on the date of declaration. A shareholder holds 10 shares.
**Option 1 — cash dividend.** Ex-dividend price ₹200 − ₹50 = ₹150. The shareholder has ₹500 of cash (₹50 × 10) plus shares worth ₹1,500 (₹150 × 10) = ==**₹2,000**==.
**Option 2 — repurchase of ₹50 crores of shares.** At ₹200 that is 25 lakh shares, or 25% of the 1 crore outstanding, so the shareholder's 10 shares become 6 and ₹800 is received (4 shares × ₹200). Market capitalisation falls from ₹200 crores to ₹150 crores over 75 lakh shares, so ==**the price stays at ₹200**==. Wealth = ₹800 of cash + ₹1,200 of shares (6 × ₹200) = ==**₹2,000**== — the same.

==**3. Stock dividend (Bonus Shares)** — a distribution of shares in lieu of cash dividend. When the company issues new shares to its existing shareholders without any consideration it is called bonus shares; they are distributed proportionately, ==**thereby retaining proportionate ownership**==. A holder of 100 shares receiving a 10% stock dividend gets 10 more shares, ==**increasing equity share capital and reducing reserves and surplus. The total net worth is not affected, as retained earnings are only capitalised.**==

==**SEBI conditions for a bonus issue** (SM §3): **bonus shares are issued not in lieu of cash dividends**; the issue must be **authorised by the Articles of Association**; it is **not to be declared unless all partly paid-up shares have been converted into fully paid-up shares**; the company **should not have defaulted in repayment of loan, interest or any statutory dues**; and bonus shares are to be issued **only from share premium and free reserves, and not from capital reserve arising on revaluation of fixed assets**.==

==**Why companies use bonus shares to stop selling** (SM §3): short term capital gains are taxed at **15%** and long term capital gains at **10%**, and **the period of holding for bonus shares starts from the date of issue of the bonus shares**. An investor would therefore not sell bonus shares immediately, as they might lose 5% on taxation — which indirectly helps the company, because the price does not fall further from selling pressure.== ==**Update-sensitive:** these rates are the ones printed in the current edition; check the edition in force for the January 2027 attempt before quoting them.==

==**Advantages of stock dividend.** **To shareholders:** (a) **no tax is payable by shareholders** on stock dividend received from a domestic company, as it is treated not as dividend but as a **capital asset** under the Income Tax Act, 1961; (b) a policy of paying a **fixed dividend per share** continued after a stock dividend will **increase total cash dividend** in future; (c) bonus shares **improve liquidity in the hands of shareholders**, by breaking higher priced shares into lower priced shares so that some can be sold. **To the company:** (a) **conservation of cash** for profitable investment opportunities; (b) suitable in case of **cash deficiency and restrictions imposed by lenders** on paying cash dividend.==

==**Limitations of stock dividend.** **To shareholders:** it **does not affect the wealth of shareholders and therefore has no value for them** — the declaration is a method of **capitalising past earnings** and a formal way of recognising earnings the shareholders already own. It merely divides the company's ownership into a larger number of share certificates; ==**James Porterfield regards stock dividends as a division of corporate pie into a larger number of pieces**==. Proportionate ownership does not change at all, though it **creates a favourable psychological impact** as an indication of growth. **To the company:** stock dividends are **costlier to administer than cash dividends**, and it is disadvantageous if **periodic small stock dividends** are declared.

official_questions.question: MENTION any one advantage of stock dividend — to the company as well as to the investor. (2 Marks)
answer_points: ==**To the investor (shareholder).** **No tax is payable by shareholders on a stock dividend received from a domestic company**, because it is treated not as dividend but as a **capital asset** under the Income Tax Act, 1961 — so the benefit arrives untaxed at the time of receipt.==

Any one of ICAI's other two shareholder advantages also answers: a policy of paying a **fixed dividend per share**, continued after the stock dividend, **increases the total cash dividend** in future, because there are now more shares; and bonus shares **improve liquidity**, since a high-priced share is broken into lower-priced shares that can be sold in part.
==**To the company.** **Conservation of cash for meeting profitable investment opportunities** — the shareholders are rewarded without any cash leaving the business.==
ICAI's second company advantage is equally available: a stock dividend is **suitable in case of cash deficiency and where lenders have imposed restrictions on paying cash dividend**.

**The two-mark discipline.** The question asks for **one** of each, so give one shareholder advantage and one company advantage, each in a single labelled sentence. ==Listing all five earns the same two marks and costs three minutes.==
official_questions.conclusion: To the investor: no tax, because it is a capital asset rather than dividend. To the company: cash is conserved for investment.

official_questions.question: EXPLAIN any common form of dividend. (2 Marks)
answer_points: ==**Cash dividend is the most common form of dividend.** 'Cash' here means **cash, cheque, warrant, demand draft, pay order or payment directly through Electronic Clearing Service (ECS)** — ==**but not in kind**==.

**Why it is the default form.** It converts part of profit after tax directly into money in the shareholder's hands. Its cost is that it **reduces the company's cash** and so the funds available for profitable investment, and it drives the share to its **ex-dividend price** on the following day.

**If the question is read as inviting more than one form**, the other two are: **share repurchase**, where the company buys back its own shares with corporate cash, the shares being held as **treasury shares** for re-issue or **cancelled** and retired — and ICAI notes that, other things equal, **its effect on shareholders' wealth is the same as a cash dividend**; and **stock dividend (bonus shares)**, a distribution of shares in lieu of cash, which **capitalises reserves without affecting total net worth**.

**The answer in two marks.** Name cash dividend, say precisely what cash includes and that it excludes payment in kind, and add one line on its effect. ==Naming the form without ICAI's own list of instruments is the half-mark most often lost here.==
official_questions.conclusion: Cash dividend — cash, cheque, warrant, demand draft, pay order or ECS, but never in kind.

mcqs.question: HM Ltd has 1 crore shares quoted at ₹200 and will return ₹50 crores to shareholders, either as a ₹50 dividend per share or by repurchasing shares at ₹200. For a holder of 10 shares, the wealth after the event is:

options.A: ₹2,000 under the dividend and ₹1,200 under the repurchase
options.B: ₹1,500 under the dividend and ₹2,000 under the repurchase
options.C: ₹2,000 under either route
options.D: ₹2,000 under the dividend and ₹2,400 under the repurchase

mcqs.explanation: SM §3: under the dividend the ex-dividend price is ₹150, so the holder has ₹500 of cash and ₹1,500 of shares. Under the repurchase, 25 lakh of the 1 crore shares go, so 4 of the 10 are sold for ₹800, market capitalisation falls from ₹200 crores to ₹150 crores over 75 lakh shares leaving the price at ₹200, and the 6 remaining shares are worth ₹1,200. Both routes give ₹2,000, which is why ICAI says the effect on shareholders' wealth is the same.

why_wrong.A: ₹1,200 is only the share component of the repurchase route; the ₹800 of cash is part of the wealth too.
why_wrong.B: ₹1,500 is only the share component of the dividend route.
why_wrong.D: No route creates wealth; returning cash cannot.

mcqs.trap: In the dividend route the price falls and the share count is unchanged; in the repurchase route the price is unchanged and the share count falls. Count the cash in both.

mcqs.question: Under the SEBI conditions set out in the study material, a bonus issue may be made out of:

options.A: Capital reserve arising on revaluation of fixed assets
options.B: The current year's profit before tax
options.C: Any reserve, provided the Articles of Association permit it
options.D: Share premium and free reserves

mcqs.explanation: SM §3: bonus shares are to be issued only from share premium and free reserves and not from capital reserve on account of fixed assets revaluation. The issue must also be authorised by the Articles, must not be in lieu of cash dividend, requires all partly paid shares to be made fully paid, and is barred where the company has defaulted on loan, interest or statutory dues.

why_wrong.B: A bonus issue capitalises reserves, not the current year's pre-tax profit.
why_wrong.C: Authorisation by the Articles is a separate condition and does not widen the permitted sources.

mcqs.trap: Authorisation by the Articles is necessary but not sufficient — the source of the reserve matters independently.

recap: Three forms: cash dividend, share repurchase, and stock dividend (bonus shares).
Cash means cash, cheque, warrant, draft, pay order or ECS — never in kind.
Cash dividend and share repurchase leave shareholders' wealth the same; HM Ltd's ₹2,000 proves it.
A bonus issue capitalises reserves out of share premium and free reserves only, leaving net worth unchanged.

concepts.title: 4–5 Significance of Dividend Policy, and Retained Earnings and Growth
understand: ==**Dividend policy is governed by two decisions** (SM §4): the **long term financing decision** and the **wealth maximization decision**.==

==**(i) Long Term Financing Decision.** Equity can be raised **externally** through a new issue or generated **internally** through retained earnings, and ==**retained earnings are preferable because they do not involve any floatation costs**==. Payment of cash dividend reduces the funds available to finance profitable investment opportunities, thereby **restricting financing options**. The decision therefore rests on two questions: ==**1. Does the organisation have opportunities in hand to invest the profit, if retained? 2. Will the return on such investment (ROI) be higher than the expectations of shareholders, i.e. Ke?**==

==**(ii) Wealth Maximization Decision.** The problem is what **Dividend Payout ratio (D/P)** to set in relation to the **Market price of the shares (MPS)**. ICAI gives two grounds: **because of market imperfections and uncertainty, shareholders give more importance to near dividends than to future dividends and capital gains**, so payment of dividends **influences the market price directly** — ==**higher dividends increase the value of shares and low dividends decrease it**== — and **a proper balance has to be struck between these two approaches**.==

==And the counterweight: **when the firm increases its retained earnings, shareholders' dividends decrease and the market price is affected**; but **use of retained earnings to finance profitable investments increases the future earnings per share**, because shareholders expect those investments to produce higher returns later. **On the other hand, an increase in dividends may cause the firm to forego investment opportunities for lack of funds and thereby decrease future earnings per share.**==

==ICAI's conclusion: **management should develop a dividend policy which divides net earnings into dividends and retained earnings in an optimum way so as to achieve the objective of wealth maximization for shareholders** — a policy influenced by the investment opportunities available and by the value of dividends against capital gains to shareholders.==

==**§5 Relationship between retained earnings and growth.** It is captured in one equation: ==**Growth (g) = br**==, where **g** is the growth rate of the firm, **b** the **retention ratio** and **r** the **rate of return on investment**.==

**SM Example 1, which is the whole of §5.** A Ltd and B Ltd each have capital employed of ₹50,00,000 in equity shares of ₹100, each earning 20%, with the same capital structure and the same ROI but different dividend policy. A Ltd distributes **100%** of earnings; B Ltd distributes **50%**.

| | A Ltd | B Ltd |
|---|---|---|
| Previous year earnings @ 20% | ₹10,00,000 | ₹10,00,000 |
| Dividend | ₹10,00,000 | ₹5,00,000 |
| Retained earnings | Nil | ₹5,00,000 |
| Capital employed next year | ₹50,00,000 | ₹55,00,000 |
| **Earnings next year @ 20%** | **₹10,00,000** | **₹11,00,000** |

==B Ltd's earnings grow 10%, which is exactly **b × r = 0.50 × 20% = 10%**. A Ltd, retaining nothing, grows at **0 × 20% = 0%**.==

That identity is the hinge of the whole chapter. **Gordon's denominator is Ke − br, so every change in the payout ratio changes the growth rate as well as the dividend** — which is why in Gordon's model a higher payout can lower the price even though more cash is being handed over.

concepts.title: 6 Determinants of Dividend Decisions
understand: ==**Nine factors affect the dividend policy** (SM §6):==

==**1. Availability of funds** — if the business needs funds, retained earnings could be a good source, because they **save floatation cost and prevent dilution of control** which a new public issue would cause. **2. Cost of capital** — if the financing requirement is to be met through **debt**, a relatively cheaper source, it would be preferable to **distribute more dividend**; if through a **fresh issue of equity**, it is better to use retained earnings as much as possible. **3. Capital structure** — an **optimum debt-equity ratio** should also be considered.==

==**4. Stock price** — meaning market price of the shares: generally **higher dividends increase market value and low dividends decrease the value**. **5. Investment opportunities in hand** — if there are opportunities, the company may prefer to **retain more earnings**. **6. Trend of industry** — investors depend on some industries for regular dividend income, so in such cases **firms have to pay dividend in order to survive in the market**.==

==**7. Expectation of shareholders** — shareholders fall into two categories, **those who invest for regular income and those who invest for growth**, and ==**generally the investor prefers current dividend over the future growth**==.==

==**8. Legal constraints — Section 123 of the Companies Act, 2013.** Dividend shall be declared or paid by a company for any financial year **only**: **(a)** out of the profits of the company for that year arrived at after providing for depreciation; **(b)** out of the profits of any previous financial year or years arrived at after providing for depreciation and remaining undistributed; **(c)** out of both; or **(d)** out of money provided by the Central Government or a State Government for the payment of dividend in pursuance of a guarantee given by that Government.==
==And a proviso worth quoting: while computing profits for payment of dividends, **any amount representing unrealised gains, notional gains or revaluation of assets, and any change in the carrying amount of an asset or a liability on measurement at fair value, shall be excluded**.==

==**9. Taxation.** Before 1st April 2020, under Section 115-O of the Income Tax Act, 1961, dividend was subject to **dividend distribution tax (DDT) in the hands of the company**, and dividend on which DDT was paid was exempt in the hands of the shareholder under section 10(34). By the amendment made by the **Finance Act 2020**, the exemption under section 10(34) does not apply to dividend received on or after **1st April 2020**, and dividend income from shares held as investment is **taxable under the head 'Other income' at the applicable slab rate**. ==**In short, dividend is now taxable in the hands of the investor.**==== ==**Update-sensitive:** the taxation and legal paragraphs follow the edition in force; verify them against the edition applicable to the January 2027 attempt.==

**How to hold nine factors.** Six of them are internal money questions — can we fund it, what does funding cost, what does it do to the capital structure, what does it do to the price, do we have somewhere better to put it, what do our shareholders want. The other three are external constraints — the industry's habit, the Companies Act, and the tax code.

concepts.title: 7 Practical Considerations in Dividend Policy, the Payout Policies and Lintner's Model
understand: ==ICAI frames the whole section around two questions: **should there be a stable pattern of dividends over the years, or should the company treat each dividend decision completely independent?**==

==**(a) Financial Needs of a Company.** Retained earnings can be a source of finance for creating profitable investment opportunities, and ==**when the rate of return of a company is greater than the return required by shareholders, it would be advantageous for the shareholders to re-invest their earnings**==. Risk and financial obligations increase if a company raises capital through an issue of new shares, where floatation costs are involved.==

**ICAI's comparison of mature against growth companies, printed as a table and asked as a differentiate question:**

| Mature Companies | Growth Companies |
|---|---|
| Having few investment opportunities, they show **high payout ratios** | Have **low payout ratios**; they need funds to finance fast growing fixed assets |
| Share prices are **sensitive to any change in dividend payout** | Distribution of earnings reduces the company's funds, so they **retain all the earnings and declare bonus shares** to offset shareholders' dividend requirements |
| **A small portion of the earnings is kept** to meet emergent and occasional financial needs | They **increase the amount of dividends gradually as profitable investment opportunities start falling** |

==**(b) Constraints on Paying Dividends** — four of them. **(i) Legal:** section 123, as set out under the determinants. **(ii) Liquidity:** payment of dividends means outflow of cash, so the ability to pay depends on the cash and liquidity position; a **mature company** has few investment opportunities and no funds tied up in permanent working capital, so it has a sound cash position, while a **growth oriented company**, despite good profits, needs funds to expand operations and permanent working capital and is **less likely to declare dividends**.==

==**(iii) Access to the Capital Market:** by paying large dividends the cash position is affected, so if new shares have to be issued to finance investment programmes and the existing shareholders cannot buy additional shares, **their control is diluted** — in which case payment of dividends may be withheld and earnings used for financing. **(iv) Investment Opportunities:** if investment opportunities are **inadequate**, it is better to **pay dividends and raise external funds** whenever necessary for such opportunities.==

==**(c) Payout policies**, which can be maintained by fixing the amount or rate of dividend irrespective of earnings. **(i) Constant Dividend Policy:** shareholders are given a **fixed amount of dividend irrespective of actual earnings**. To maintain it, a reserve such as a **Dividend Equalisation Reserve Fund**, earmarked by marketable securities, is created out of surplus earnings of good years and used to pay dividends in bad ones. ==**This policy treats common shareholders at par with preference shareholders**== without giving them any preferred opportunities within the firm, and is preferred by persons and institutions that depend on dividend income to meet living and operating expenses. ==**Companies that use a constant dividend policy find their dividend fluctuates with earnings in the short term.**==

==**(ii) Stable Dividend Policy:** the ratio of dividend to earnings is the **payout ratio**, and some companies follow a **constant payout ratio** — a fixed percentage of net earnings every year. ICAI quotes Infosys Technologies' 2011 annual report: *'The Dividend Policy is to distribute up to 30% of the Consolidated Profit after Tax (PAT) of the Infosys Group as Dividend.'* And against it, **Warren Buffet**: *'We will either pay large dividends or none at all if we can't obtain more money through re-investment (of those funds). There is no logic to regularly paying out 10% or 20% of earnings as dividends every year.'*==

==Under a constant payout ratio **the amount of dividend fluctuates in direct proportion to earnings**: at a 40% payout, 40 paise of every rupee of net earnings is paid out, so ₹2 of EPS gives 80 paise of dividend and ₹1.50 gives 60 paise. **For losses incurred, no dividend shall be paid.** Internal financing with retained earnings is automatic, the policy is **conservative** and **provides a guarantee against over- or under-payment**. ==Companies that use a stable dividend policy **base dividend on a long-term forecast of sustainable earnings and increase dividends when earnings have increased to a substantially higher level**.==

==**Lintner's Model**, which the study material places here rather than among the §8 theories. ==**It has two parameters: (i) the target payout ratio, and (ii) the spread at which current dividends adjust to the target.**== John Lintner based the model on a series of interviews with corporate managers in the mid 1950s.==

==**Lintner's four assumptions:** **1.** Firms have a **long term dividend payout ratio** and maintain a fixed payout over the long term — mature companies with stable earnings may have high payouts and growth companies usually low payouts. **2.** ==**Managers are more concerned with changes in dividends than the absolute amounts of dividends**== — a manager may easily decide to pay ₹2 if last year it was ₹2, but paying ₹3 where last year's was ₹2 is an important financial management decision. **3.** **Dividend changes follow changes in long run sustainable earnings. 4. Managers are reluctant to affect dividend changes that may have to be reversed.**==

==**The formula.** Under Lintner's model, the current year's dividend depends on the current year's earnings **and last year's dividend**:
==**D₁ = D₀ + [(EPS × Target payout) − D₀] × Af**==
where **D₁** is the dividend in year 1, **D₀** the dividend in year 0 (last year's dividend), **EPS** earnings per share and ==**Af the adjustment factor or speed of adjustment**==.

**How to read the formula in one line.** The term in brackets is **the full gap between what the target payout would pay and what was paid last year**; the adjustment factor says **what fraction of that gap is closed this year**. An Af of 1 moves straight to the target; an Af of 0 never moves at all. That is assumption 4 made arithmetical.
concepts.example: A company paid ₹2 last year, earns EPS of ₹5, has a target payout of 60% and an adjustment factor of 0.5. The target dividend is ₹3; the gap is ₹1; half of it is closed, so this year's dividend is ₹2 + ₹0.50 = ₹2.50. The company moves towards its target without committing to a level it may have to reverse.

official_questions.question: DISCUSS the parameters of Lintner's Model. (2 Marks)
answer_points: ==**Lintner's model has two parameters** (SM §7(c)): **(i) the target payout ratio**, and **(ii) the spread at which current dividends adjust to the target.**==

**What each parameter does.** The **target payout ratio** is the long-run proportion of earnings the firm intends to distribute — mature companies with stable earnings may set it high, growth companies low. The **spread, or speed of adjustment**, is how quickly the company moves from the dividend it actually paid last year to the dividend the target would imply this year.

==**The formula that puts both to work:** ==**D₁ = D₀ + [(EPS × Target payout) − D₀] × Af**== where D₁ is this year's dividend, D₀ last year's dividend, EPS earnings per share and **Af the adjustment factor or speed of adjustment**. ==The bracket is the **whole gap** between the target dividend and last year's; **Af is the fraction of that gap closed this year**.==

**Where the model comes from, and the behaviour it captures.** John Lintner built it from interviews with corporate managers in the mid 1950s, and it rests on four observations: firms maintain a long term payout ratio; ==**managers are more concerned with changes in dividends than with the absolute amounts**==; dividend changes follow changes in long run sustainable earnings; and **managers are reluctant to make dividend changes that may have to be reversed**.

**That last assumption is what the adjustment factor expresses arithmetically.** An Af of 1 jumps straight to the target and risks a reversal next year; a low Af edges towards it. ==Under Lintner's model the current year's dividend therefore depends on **both** the current year's earnings and last year's dividend — which is what distinguishes it from Walter and Gordon, where last year's dividend plays no part at all.==
official_questions.conclusion: Two parameters — the target payout ratio and the speed at which dividends adjust towards it — combined in D₁ = D₀ + [(EPS × Target payout) − D₀] × Af.

concepts.title: 8–8.1 Theories of Dividend and the Dividend Irrelevance Theory (MM Hypothesis)
concepts.evidence: PYQ 2 (Jan 2026 Q1(c), May 2026 Q4(a)) · RTP 2 (May 2024, Sep 2026) · MTP 6 (Jan 2025 S1, Jan 2026 S1 and S2, Mar 2024 S2, May 2025 S1 and S2)
understand: ==**Modigliani – Miller theory was proposed by Franco Modigliani and Merton Miller in 1961.** ==**MM approach is in support of the irrelevance of dividends, i.e. a firm's dividend policy has no effect on either the price of the firm's stock or its cost of capital.**==

==**According to MM Hypothesis** (SM §8.1): **the market value of the equity shares of a firm depends solely on its earning power and is not influenced by the manner in which its earnings are split between dividends and retained earnings**; the **market value of equity shares is not affected by dividend size**; and ==**under MM hypothesis there is no meaningful distinction between dividend and share repurchases — they are both ways for a company to return cash to shareholders**==.

==**Five assumptions** (SM §8.1): **Perfect capital markets** — all investors are rational and information is freely available to all. **No taxes** — no tax discrimination between dividend income and capital appreciation, an assumption necessary for universal applicability since tax rates differ between countries. **Fixed investment policy** — all investment is financed through equity only, since the implication of using debt may be difficult to understand and the impact differs case by case. **No floatation or transaction cost**. ==**Risk of uncertainty does not exist** — investors can forecast future prices and dividends with certainty, and one discount rate is appropriate for all securities and all time periods.==

==**Three situations under MM Hypothesis.** **1. Firm pays cash dividends from Reserve & Surplus:** shareholders receive cash, reducing the firm's cash balance — ==**only a transfer of asset (cash) from one pocket to another pocket of the shareholders, with no net gain or loss**==, so the value of the firm is unaffected. **2. Firm pays cash dividends from a new issue of shares:** lacking cash, the firm issues new shares and uses the proceeds to pay the dividend; shareholders receive cash **but suffer an equal capital loss from dilution of control over the assets and dilution in earnings per share**, so there is no change in wealth. **3. Firm does not pay any dividend:** a shareholder wanting cash **sells part of his shareholding**, and the cash received is known as a ==**'home-made dividend'**==; again a capital receipt offset by a capital loss from dilution, so no gain or loss.==

==**The pricing relation, which MM builds on the arbitrage argument:**
==**P₀ = (P₁ + D₁) ÷ (1 + Ke)**==
where **P₀** is the price at the beginning of the period, **P₁** the price at the end, **D₁** the dividend at the end and **Ke** the cost of equity / rate of capitalization / discount rate. Rearranged for exam use: ==**P₁ = P₀(1 + Ke) − D₁**==.

==**And the value of the firm:**
==**Vf or nP₀ = [(n + Δn)P₁ − I + E] ÷ (1 + Ke)**==
where **n** is the number of shares at the beginning, **Δn** the number of shares issued to raise the funds required, **I** the amount required for investment and **E** the total earnings during the period.==

==**Where Δn comes from**, which is the step most often fumbled: retained earnings = **E − nD₁**, so the funds that must be raised are **I − (E − nD₁)**, and
==**Δn = [I − (E − nD₁)] ÷ P₁**==, i.e. **ΔnP₁ = I − (E − nD₁)**.==

**SM Example 2, the shortest demonstration in the chapter.** Dev Ltd has 2 lakh shares at ₹10, no borrowings, all retained earnings already used for capital expenditure, a constant dividend of ₹3 a share and Ke of 10%.
**(i) Dividends not paid:** P₁ = 10(1.10) − 0 = **₹11**; value of firm = ₹11 × 2,00,000 = **₹22,00,000**.
**(ii) Dividends paid:** P₁ = 10(1.10) − 3 = **₹8**; new shares to be issued = total dividend ÷ P₁ = (2,00,000 × ₹3) ÷ ₹8 = **75,000 shares**; value of firm = ₹8 × 2,75,000 = **₹22,00,000**. ==The value is the same either way.==

==**Advantages of MM Hypothesis:** the model is **logically consistent**, and it **provides a satisfactory framework on dividend policy with the concept of the arbitrage process**. **Limitations:** the **validity of the various assumptions is questionable**, and the model **may not be valid under uncertainty**.==

**SM Illustration 1, the template every MM question in the official set follows.** AB Engineering Ltd, capitalization rate 10%, 10,000 shares at ₹100, contemplating a ₹5 dividend, net income ₹1,00,000, new investments ₹2,00,000. Case 1 (no dividend): P₁ = 100(1.10) = ₹110; Δn = (₹2,00,000 − ₹1,00,000) ÷ ₹110 = 909.09 shares; value = [(10,909.09 × ₹110) − ₹2,00,000 + ₹1,00,000] ÷ 1.10 = **₹10,00,000**. Case 2 (dividend of ₹5): P₁ = 110 − 5 = ₹105; Δn = [₹2,00,000 − (₹1,00,000 − ₹50,000)] ÷ ₹105 = 1,428.57 shares; value = [(11,428.57 × ₹105) − ₹2,00,000 + ₹1,00,000] ÷ 1.10 = **₹10,00,000**. Same both ways.

official_questions.question: MM Hypothesis of dividend policy is based on certain assumptions. What are those assumptions without which the hypothesis cannot hold? Explain briefly. (4 Marks)
answer_points: ==**1. Perfect capital markets.** The firm operates in a market in which **all investors are rational and information is freely available to all**. Without it, investors could not substitute a home-made dividend for a declared one at no cost, and the arbitrage argument would fail.==

==**2. No taxes.** There are **no taxes and no tax discrimination between dividend income and capital appreciation (capital gain)** — the taxation of the two is identical. ICAI gives the reason expressly: **this assumption is necessary for the universal applicability of the theory, since tax rates may be different in different countries.**==

==**3. Fixed investment policy.** It is necessary to assume that **all investment is financed through equity only**, since the implications of using debt as a source of finance may be difficult to understand and the impact would be different in different cases.==

==**4. No floatation or transaction cost.** Similarly, these costs **may differ from country to country or market to market**. Without the assumption, issuing shares to fund a dividend would destroy value and the irrelevance result would break.==

==**5. Risk of uncertainty does not exist.** **Investors are able to forecast future prices and dividends with certainty, and one discount rate is appropriate for all securities and all time periods.**==

**Why each one is load-bearing, which is what 'without which the hypothesis cannot hold' asks.** The whole proof is that a shareholder can manufacture any dividend stream by buying or selling shares. ==**Taxes make the two routes unequal; transaction costs make the substitution expensive; uncertainty makes a future price worth less than a present dividend; a variable investment policy means the dividend decision changes the investment decision.** Remove any one assumption and dividend policy starts to matter — which is exactly the ground Walter and Gordon occupy.==

**A closing line that reads as understanding rather than recall.** ICAI's own limitations of the model are that the **validity of the various assumptions is questionable** and that the **model may not be valid under uncertainty** — so the assumptions are not incidental scaffolding but the whole of the result.
official_questions.conclusion: Perfect capital markets, no taxes, fixed investment policy, no floatation or transaction cost, and no risk of uncertainty — each necessary because the proof depends on a shareholder being able to replicate any dividend policy costlessly.
keywords: risk of uncertainty does not exist

official_questions.question: MCO Ltd. has a paid-up share capital of ₹10,00,000, face value ₹10 each. The current market price of the shares is ₹20 each. The Board has an agenda to pay a dividend of 25% to its shareholders. The company expects a net income of ₹5,20,000 at the end of the current financial year, and plans capital expenditure of ₹7,50,000 next year, financed through retained earnings and an issue of new equity shares. The company's desired rate of investment is 15%. Following the Modigliani-Miller hypothesis, determine the value of the company when (i) it does not pay dividend and (ii) it does pay dividend. (ICAI label: Dividend Decision.)
answer_points: ==**Conclusion.** The value of the company is **₹20,00,000 in both cases** — which is also simply n × P₀ = 1,00,000 × ₹20. **Dividend policy is therefore irrelevant to the value of the firm**, exactly as the MM hypothesis holds.==

**The structural insight worth stating in the answer.** Notice what is identical in the two computations: **(n + Δn)P₁ comes to ₹25,30,000 either way.** Paying the dividend lowers P₁ by exactly the dividend per share and raises Δn by exactly enough to compensate — ==**the two effects are algebraically bound to cancel, which is why the result is not a coincidence of these figures but a property of the formula**==.

**On the fractional share.** Δn of 23,414.63 is not a whole number, and ICAI does not round it; leaving the decimal in keeps the value at exactly ₹20,00,000 and demonstrates the point. If a question asks for the number of shares as an answer in itself, say that it would be rounded up in practice.
official_questions.conclusion: ₹20,00,000 either way — and (n + Δn)P₁ is ₹25,30,000 under both policies, which is why the values must agree.

official_questions.question: M Ltd. belongs to a risk class for which the capitalization rate is 12%. It has 40,000 outstanding shares and the current market price is ₹200. It expects a net profit of ₹5,00,000 for the year and the Board is considering a dividend of ₹10 per share. M Ltd. requires to raise ₹10,00,000 for an approved investment expenditure. Illustrate how the MM approach affects the value of M Ltd. if dividends are paid or not paid. (5 Marks)
answer_points: ==**Conclusion.** The value of M Ltd. is **₹80,00,000 whether or not the dividend is paid** — and that is simply 40,000 × ₹200. **Under the MM approach the dividend decision does not affect the value of the firm.**==

**The same cancellation as in MCO Ltd, worth noticing once and then relied on.** (n + Δn)P₁ = **₹94,60,000** under both policies. ==Paying ₹4,00,000 of dividend cuts the year-end price by ₹10 and forces ₹4,00,000 more of new issue; the extra shares are worth precisely the fall in value of the old ones.==

**What the word 'Illustrate' is asking for.** Not just the two numbers but the demonstration: compute both, show they are equal, and say in a sentence that this is the MM result. ==A pair of correct figures without that sentence answers the arithmetic and not the question.==

**A practical check available in every MM question.** Since the value of the firm must come to **n × P₀**, you can verify the whole computation in one multiplication before writing the conclusion — here 40,000 × ₹200 = ₹80,00,000.
official_questions.conclusion: ₹80,00,000 with or without the dividend, equal to n × P₀ — the MM irrelevance result.
keywords: dividend decision does not affect value

official_questions.question: Perfact Ltd. has 8 lakh equity shares outstanding at the beginning of the year. The current market price per share is ₹120. The Board is contemplating ₹6.4 per share as dividend. The rate of capitalisation appropriate to the risk class to which the company belongs is 9.6%. (i) Based on the M-M approach, calculate the market price of the share when the dividend is (a) declared and (b) not declared. (ii) Determine how many new shares are to be issued if the company desires to fund an investment budget of ₹3.20 crores by the end of the year, assuming net income for the year will be ₹1.60 crores. (5 Marks)
answer_points: ==**(ii) New shares, if the dividend is declared.** Total dividend = 8,00,000 × ₹6.40 = **₹51.20 lakhs**. Retained earnings = ₹160 lakhs − ₹51.20 lakhs = **₹108.80 lakhs**. Funds to be raised = ₹320 lakhs − ₹108.80 lakhs = **₹211.20 lakhs**, so **Δn = ₹2,11,20,000 ÷ ₹125.12 = 1,68,798 shares** (approximately).==

==**And if the dividend is not declared.** Retained earnings = the whole ₹160 lakhs, so funds to be raised = ₹320 lakhs − ₹160 lakhs = **₹160 lakhs**, and **Δn = ₹1,60,00,000 ÷ ₹131.52 = 1,21,655 shares** (approximately).==

**The cross-check, in one line.** Value of the firm = n × P₀ = 8,00,000 × ₹120 = **₹9.60 crores** on either policy. Confirm it with the formula if the question asks: [(8,00,000 + 1,68,798) × ₹125.12 − ₹320 lakhs + ₹160 lakhs] ÷ 1.096 ≈ ₹9.60 crores.

==**Why the two Δn figures differ so much — 1.69 lakh shares against 1.22 lakh.** Paying the dividend takes ₹51.20 lakhs out of the business, so ₹51.20 lakhs more has to be raised; and it is raised at a **lower** price (₹125.12 rather than ₹131.52), so more shares are needed for each rupee. **Both effects push the same way**, which is why the dividend route always needs materially more new shares.==

**A caution on the capitalisation rate.** 9.6% is unusual enough to be mistyped as 9% or 10%; ₹120 × 1.096 = ₹131.52 is the figure the whole answer rests on, so it is worth writing out rather than doing in the head.
official_questions.conclusion: P₁ of ₹125.12 with the dividend and ₹131.52 without; about 1,68,798 new shares if the dividend is declared and 1,21,655 if it is not.
keywords: new shares at the year-end price

official_questions.question: SOC Ltd has 10 lakh equity shares outstanding at the beginning of the accounting year 2024. The existing market price per share is ₹600. Expected dividend is ₹40 per share. The rate of capitalization appropriate to the risk class to which the company belongs is 20%. (i) Calculate the market price per share by the end of the year when expected dividends are (a) declared and (b) not declared, based on the Miller-Modigliani approach. (ii) Calculate the number of shares to be issued by the company at the end of the accounting year on the assumption that the net income for the year is ₹15 crore and the investment budget is ₹20 crores, when (a) dividends are declared and (b) dividends are not declared.
answer_points: ==**(ii)(a) Dividends declared.** Total dividend = 10,00,000 × ₹40 = **₹4 crores**. Retained earnings = ₹15 crores − ₹4 crores = **₹11 crores**. Funds to be raised = ₹20 crores − ₹11 crores = **₹9 crores**, so **Δn = ₹9,00,00,000 ÷ ₹680 = 1,32,353 shares** (approximately).==
==**(ii)(b) Dividends not declared.** Retained earnings = ₹15 crores; funds to be raised = ₹20 crores − ₹15 crores = **₹5 crores**; **Δn = ₹5,00,00,000 ÷ ₹720 = 69,444 shares** (approximately).==
**Value of the firm, if asked.** n × P₀ = 10,00,000 × ₹600 = **₹60 crores** on either policy.

==**The arithmetic lesson of the pair.** The dividend costs ₹4 crores of internal funds and it also cuts the issue price from ₹720 to ₹680 — so the number of new shares nearly doubles, from about 69,000 to about 1,32,000. **Under MM that dilution is exactly what cancels the dividend in the shareholder's hands**; outside MM's assumptions, floatation cost and taxes would make it a real loss, which is the opening Walter and Gordon exploit.==
**On rounding.** Neither Δn is whole. State the figure to the nearest share and note that in practice the issue would be rounded up, with the small excess adding to cash.
official_questions.conclusion: P₁ ₹680 with the dividend and ₹720 without; about 1,32,353 new shares if declared and 69,444 if not.
keywords: number of shares to be issued

official_questions.question: The stocks of Firms A and B are considered to be equally risky. Investors expect the share of Firm A, which does not intend to pay any dividend, to be worth ₹100 one year from now. Investors expect a total payoff of ₹100 from the share of Firm B after one year, comprising ₹10 as dividend income and ₹90 as the expected share price. Dividends are taxed at 25% and capital gains at 12%. Assuming each stock is expected to provide a post-tax rate of return of 18% and that the radical position holds, determine the current market prices of the shares of Firms A and B. (ICAI label: Dividend decision.)
answer_points: ==**What the 'radical position' is, since the current Study Material does not carry it.** It is the **tax-differential view** of dividend policy: where **dividends are taxed more heavily than capital gains**, investors require a higher pre-tax return on a share that pays dividend, so **a high-payout share is worth less than an otherwise identical low-payout share**. It is the mirror image of Gordon's bird-in-hand argument and a direct attack on MM's 'no taxes' assumption.==

==**Set up one equation per firm**: the price today, grown at the required post-tax return, must equal the price today plus the post-tax dividend plus the post-tax capital gain.
**Firm A** — no dividend, so the whole return is capital gain taxed at 12%:
1.18A = A + 0.88 × (₹100 − A) → 1.18A = A + 88 − 0.88A → **1.06A = 88** → ==**A = ₹83.02**==.

==**The conclusion the question is driving at.** Both shares promise the **same ₹100 of pre-tax payoff** in a year and carry the **same risk**, yet **Firm A is worth ₹83.02 and Firm B only ₹81.79**. The ₹1.23 difference is entirely the tax penalty on Firm B's ₹10 of dividend: ₹10 taxed at 25% rather than at 12% costs ₹1.30 of post-tax income, which discounted back is about ₹1.10 — and the rest follows from the grossing up.==

**Why this belongs under §8.1 even though it contradicts it.** MM's irrelevance result is built on the assumption that **there is no tax discrimination between dividend income and capital appreciation**. This question removes exactly that assumption and nothing else — and dividend policy immediately matters. ==**It is the cleanest possible demonstration that MM's conclusion is a consequence of its assumptions rather than of the arithmetic.**==

**For the exam.** Reproduce the two equations as ICAI does, labelling the unknowns A and B. ==**The theory is not in the Study Material, so a question on it would have to supply the method, as this one does by naming the radical position; it is the computation that is examinable.**==
official_questions.conclusion: Firm A ₹83.02 and Firm B ₹81.79 — identical payoffs and risk, and the dividend-paying share is worth ₹1.23 less because its return is taxed more heavily.

official_questions.question: Under Modigliani and Miller's Dividend Irrelevance Theory, what happens to shareholder wealth when a company changes its dividend policy? The options offered included that it rises, that it falls, that it remains unchanged because value depends on earnings and investment policy, and that it depends on the dividend payout ratio.
answer_points: ==**ICAI's key: option (c) — 'Remains unchanged because value depends on earnings and investment policy.'** Its own explanation: *'M&M's theory suggests that dividend policy has no impact on shareholder wealth in a perfect market.'*==

**The reasoning in SM's own words.** The market value of equity shares **depends solely on the firm's earning power and is not influenced by the manner in which earnings are split between dividends and retained earnings**; the market value is **not affected by dividend size**.

**Why the option names 'earnings and investment policy'.** Those are the two things MM holds fixed. ==Earning power sets the numerator and the **fixed investment policy** assumption holds the investment programme constant — so the only variable left, the dividend, has nothing to work on.==

**Why option (d) is the attractive wrong answer.** It is true under **Walter and Gordon**, where the payout ratio changes the price through the r-against-Ke comparison. ==Read which theory the question names before answering: the same question stem with 'Walter's Model' in place of 'MM' would have the opposite key.==
**The two-mark discipline.** This is a one-line recall question. The phrase to carry into the hall is **'value depends solely on earning power'**.
official_questions.conclusion: Option (c) — wealth is unchanged, because under MM value depends on earning power and investment policy, not on the dividend split.

official_questions.question: What is the value of the firm under two alternative dividend policies? ICAI's key is ₹1,00,00,000 for both policies.
answer_points: ==**ICAI's key: option (b) — '₹1,00,00,000 for both policies', with the explanation 'Under MM (no taxes), dividend policy does not affect firm value.'**==

**How to reach it without computing twice.** Under MM the value of the firm is **n × P₀** — the number of shares times the current market price — and neither of those changes when the Board resolves on a dividend. ==So wherever an MCQ offers the **same figure for both policies** as one of its options, that option is the MM answer.==

**The parenthesis matters.** ICAI writes '**no taxes**' because that is the assumption doing the work. Reinstate a tax differential between dividend and capital gains, as RTP September 2026's radical-position question does, and the two policies no longer give the same value.

**The trap in this family of MCQs.** Three of the four options will usually be different numbers, inviting a computation. ==Under MM the computation is unnecessary: two equal numbers is the answer, and arriving there in ten seconds leaves the time for a question that needs it.==
official_questions.conclusion: Option (b) ₹1,00,00,000 for both policies — the MM result, resting on the no-taxes assumption.

official_questions.question: A company with 2,00,000 shares at ₹100 declares a dividend of ₹20 per share, which shareholders reinvest at the ex-dividend price. How many shares will there be? ICAI's key is 2,50,000 shares.
answer_points: ==**ICAI's own working.** The **ex-dividend price is ₹80** (₹100 − ₹20). The total dividend received is **₹40,00,000** (2,00,000 shares × ₹20 per share), **which is re-invested at the rate of ₹80 per share**, giving **₹40,00,000 ÷ ₹80 = 50,000 new shares**. Total = 2,00,000 + 50,000 = ==**2,50,000 shares**==.==

**The two steps, and the order matters.** First find the **ex-dividend** price — the price at which shares trade immediately on the next day after declaration (SM §2). Only then divide the dividend by it. ==Dividing by the **cum-dividend** price of ₹100 gives 40,000 new shares and a total of 2,40,000, which is the distractor this question is built around.==

**Why the answer demonstrates MM rather than merely computing.** Market capitalisation before the dividend is 2,00,000 × ₹100 = ₹2 crores. After the dividend and the reinvestment it is 2,50,000 × ₹80 = **₹2 crores**. ==**The shareholders own more shares at a lower price and are exactly as wealthy as before** — which is the MM 'one pocket to another pocket' argument in two lines of arithmetic.==

**The same idea under a different name.** This is also what SM §3 shows with HM Ltd, and what SM §8.1 calls the **home-made dividend** read in reverse: a shareholder who does not want the cash can convert it straight back into shares and be where he started.
official_questions.conclusion: 2,50,000 shares — ₹40,00,000 of dividend reinvested at the ex-dividend price of ₹80, and market capitalisation unchanged at ₹2 crores.

mcqs.question: A share currently quoted at ₹200 belongs to a risk class whose capitalization rate is 12%. The Board declares a dividend of ₹10 per share. Under the MM approach the price at the end of the year will be:
mcqs.explanation: SM §8.1: P₀ = (P₁ + D₁) ÷ (1 + Ke), so P₁ = P₀(1 + Ke) − D₁ = ₹200 × 1.12 − ₹10 = ₹224 − ₹10 = ₹214. This is the M Ltd figure in MTP May 2025 Series I.

why_wrong.B: The price if no dividend were declared.

mcqs.question: Under the MM hypothesis, a shareholder who wants cash from a company that pays no dividend sells part of his shareholding. The study material calls the cash so received:

options.A: A capital reduction
options.B: An ex-dividend receipt
options.C: A treasury distribution
options.D: A home-made dividend

mcqs.explanation: SM §8.1, situation 3: when the firm does not pay any dividend but a shareholder wants to receive cash, the shareholder may sell part of his shareholding, and the cash received in the hands of the shareholder may be known as a 'home-made dividend'. The shareholder receives a capital receipt but suffers a capital loss from dilution, so there is no gain or loss overall.

why_wrong.A: A capital reduction is a company-level action under company law.
why_wrong.B: An ex-dividend price arises where a dividend has been declared, which is the opposite case.
why_wrong.C: Treasury shares are repurchased shares held for re-issue, from §3.

mcqs.trap: The whole irrelevance argument depends on this substitution being free — which is why 'no transaction cost' is one of the five assumptions.

recap: MM: dividend policy affects neither the share price nor the cost of capital; value depends solely on earning power.
Five assumptions: perfect capital markets, no taxes, fixed investment policy, no floatation or transaction cost, no uncertainty.
P₁ = P₀(1 + Ke) − D₁; nP₀ = [(n + Δn)P₁ − I + E] ÷ (1 + Ke); Δn = [I − (E − nD₁)] ÷ P₁.
Three situations — dividend from reserves, dividend from a new issue, and no dividend with a home-made dividend — each leaving wealth unchanged.
The value of the firm always comes back to n × P₀, which is the one-line check on every MM computation.

concepts.title: 8.2 Dividend's Relevance Theory (i) — Walter's Model
concepts.evidence: PYQ 3 (Jan 2025 Q1(c), May 2025 Q2(b), May 2026 Q3(a)) · RTP 2 (Jan 2025, Jan 2026) · MTP 6 (Jan 2026 S1, May 2025 S2, May 2026 S1, Sep 2025 S1 and S2, Sep 2026 S2)
understand:
==**Walter's formula**, which is the most examined single line in Paper 6A:
==**P = [D + (r ÷ Ke)(E − D)] ÷ Ke**==
where **P** is the market price of the share, **E** earnings per share, **D** dividend per share, **Ke** the cost of equity / rate of capitalization / discount rate, and **r** the internal rate of return / return on investment.==

==**Assumptions of Walter's Model** (SM §8.2): **all investment proposals of the firm are to be financed through retained earnings only**; **'r' and 'Ke' are constant**; **perfect capital markets** — all investors rational and information freely available; **no taxes or no tax discrimination between dividend income and capital appreciation**, an assumption necessary for universal applicability since tax rates differ between countries; **no floatation or transaction cost**; and ==**the firm has perpetual life**==.

==Professor James E. Walter's argument: **in the long run, share prices reflect only the present value of expected dividends**, and **retentions influence stock prices only through their effect on further dividends**. The formula emphasises **two factors**: **(1) dividend per share**, and **(2) the relationship between the internal rate of return and the cost of capital (the market capitalization rate)**.==

==**If the internal return on retained earnings is higher than the market capitalization rate, the value of ordinary shares would be high even if dividends are low. However, if the internal return within the business is lower than what the market expects, the value of the share would be low** — and in that case shareholders would prefer a higher dividend so that they can use the funds elsewhere in more profitable opportunities.==
==This is why Walter's Model **explains why market prices of shares of growing companies are high even though the dividend paid out is low**, and equally why the shares of some companies that pay high dividends and retain very little are also high.==

==**The r-against-Ke table, which is where the comment marks live:**==

| Company | Condition | Correlation between size of dividend and market price | Optimum dividend payout ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Growth** | **r > Ke** | **Negative** | **Zero** |
| **Constant** | **r = Ke** | **No correlation** | **Every payout ratio is optimum** |
| **Decline** | **r < Ke** | **Positive** | **100%** |

==**Growth oriented company:** able to invest the funds in a better manner, so **shareholders can accept a low dividend because the value of their share would be higher**. **Declining company:** not in a position to cover the cost of capital, so **shareholders would prefer a higher dividend to use their funds elsewhere in more profitable opportunities**.==

==**The cost of retained earnings**, which ICAI stresses in the prose: retention of profits depends on whether it is cheaper and more profitable for shareholders to have corporate earnings retained in the business or to receive them as cash dividend, so it involves ==**an opportunity cost — the benefits which shareholders forego in terms of leaving the funds in the business**==.

==**Advantages of Walter's Model:** **the formula is simple to understand and easy to compute**; and it **can envisage different possible market prices in different situations, and considers the internal rate of return, the market capitalisation rate and the dividend payout ratio in the determination of market value**. **Limitations:** the formula **does not consider all the factors affecting dividend policy and share prices**, and **determination of the market capitalisation rate is difficult**; further, it **ignores such factors as taxation, various legal and contractual obligations, management policy and attitude towards dividend policy and so on**.==

**SM Illustration 2, which proves the optimum payout is zero when r > Ke.** XYZ Ltd earns ₹10 a share with Ke 10% and r 12%. Since r > Ke the optimum payout is **zero**, and P = [0 + (0.12 ÷ 0.10)(10 − 0)] ÷ 0.10 = ==**₹120**==. Testing other ratios: at 25% payout **₹115**; at 50% **₹110**; at 75% **₹105**; at 100% **₹100**. ==The price falls steadily as the payout rises — the 'negative correlation' of the table, demonstrated.==

**SM Illustration 3, the reverse working ICAI sets again and again.** XYZ Ltd: net profit ₹30 lakhs, outstanding 12% preference shares ₹100 lakhs, 3 lakh equity shares, r 20%, Ke 16%. Earnings for equity shareholders = ₹30 lakhs − ₹12 lakhs = ₹18 lakhs, so **EPS = ₹6.00**. To hold the price at ₹42: ₹42 = [D + (0.20 ÷ 0.16)(6 − D)] ÷ 0.16 → 6.72 = 0.16D + 1.2 − 0.20D... ICAI's own line → **0.04D = 1.2 − 1.0752** → **D = ₹3.12**, so the ==**payout ratio = ₹3.12 ÷ ₹6 = 52%**==.

**Two habits that make every Walter question quick.** First, **always compute EPS as a labelled working** — net profit less preference dividend, over the number of equity shares. Second, where a **P/E ratio** is given, ==**Ke = 1 ÷ (P/E)**==; three official questions turn entirely on that substitution.

Same data, three times the price, entirely because Gordon's denominator is Ke − br and 0.165 is very close to 0.18.

official_questions.question: LP Ltd: profit before tax ₹40 lakh; tax rate 30%; equity share capital (₹10) ₹40 lakh; return on investment 18%; cost of equity 15%; dividend payout ratio 50%. Required: (i) determine the price of the equity share of the company as per Walter's Model; (ii) determine the dividend payout ratio by applying Walter's Model, assuming the price of the equity share of the company is ₹48. (3 + 2 = 5 Marks)
answer_points: ==**Step 1 — EPS, as a labelled working.** Profit before tax ₹40 lakh; less tax at 30% ₹12 lakh; **earning for equity shareholders ₹28 lakh**. Shares = ₹40 lakh ÷ ₹10 = **4 lakh**, so ==**EPS = ₹28 lakh ÷ 4 lakh = ₹7**==. Payout 50% gives **D = ₹3.50**.==

==**Step 3 — (ii) the reverse working.** Let the dividend per share be D to give a price of ₹48:
₹48 = [D + (0.18 ÷ 0.15)(₹7 − D)] ÷ 0.15
7.2 = (0.15D + 1.26 − 0.18D) ÷ 0.15 — ICAI's own line
**0.03D = 1.26 − 1.08 = 0.18**, so ==**D = ₹6**==, and the ==**D/P ratio = ₹6 ÷ ₹7 × 100 = 85.714%**==.==

==**The interpretation that earns the comment mark.** Here **r of 18% exceeds Ke of 15%**, so this is a **growth company**: the correlation between dividend and price is **negative** and the **optimum payout ratio is zero**. A higher payout therefore lowers the price — and the arithmetic bears it out, since raising the payout from 50% to 85.714% drives the price **down** from ₹51.33 to ₹48.==

**Why part (ii) is the harder two marks.** Candidates who treat it as a new computation lose time; it is the same equation with D unknown and P known. ==The whole working is three lines once EPS is in hand, and the only arithmetic risk is the ÷ 0.15 appearing twice.==

**A sanity check before writing the answer.** At a payout of zero, P would be [0 + 1.2 × 7] ÷ 0.15 = ₹56; at 100% payout, P = ₹7 ÷ 0.15 = ₹46.67. ==A target price of ₹48 must therefore need a payout close to but below 100%, and 85.714% sits exactly where it should.==
official_questions.conclusion: Price ₹51.33 at a 50% payout; a payout of 85.714% (D = ₹6) is what brings the price down to ₹48 — because with r above Ke the price moves against the payout.
keywords: r > Ke so optimum payout is zero

official_questions.question: K Ltd: net profit ₹50,00,000; 10% preference share capital at ₹100 each ₹2,00,00,000; number of equity shares outstanding 5,00,000; rate of return on investment 25%; cost of equity 15%. Required: (i) calculate EPS and the market price per equity share as per Walter's Model with a retention ratio of 20%; (ii) if the company aims to keep the market price of its equity share at ₹60 each, what retention ratio should be adopted; (iii) what would be the optimum dividend payout ratio as per Gordon's Model. (2 + 1 + 1 = 4 Marks)
answer_points: ==**Step 1 — EPS.** Net profit ₹50,00,000; less preference dividend 10% of ₹2,00,00,000 = **₹20,00,000**; **earnings for equity shareholders ₹30,00,000**; over 5,00,000 shares gives ==**EPS = ₹6**==. ==**The preference dividend is two-thirds of the way to the answer and is the single commonest omission in this question.**==

==**Step 3 — (ii) the retention ratio for a price of ₹60.** Let D be the dividend per share:
₹60 = [D + 1.6667(₹6 − D)] ÷ 0.15 → 9 = D + 10 − 1.6667D → **0.6667D = 1**, so ==**D = ₹1.50**==, a **payout of 25%** and therefore a ==**retention ratio of 75%**==.==

==**Step 4 — (iii) Gordon's optimum payout.** Since **r of 25% exceeds Ke of 15%**, the company is a growth company and under Gordon's Model the ==**optimum dividend payout ratio is zero**== — all earnings should be retained.==

==**The thread running through all three parts.** r > Ke, so **price moves inversely to payout**. Part (i) pays out 80% and gets ₹45.33; part (ii) shows that to reach ₹60 the payout must fall to 25%; part (iii) says that in the limit the payout should be nil. ==**One comparison, three answers** — and saying so in a closing sentence is what turns three computations into an answer.==

**A useful bracket to carry.** At zero payout P = [0 + 1.6667 × 6] ÷ 0.15 = **₹66.67**; at 100% payout P = ₹6 ÷ 0.15 = **₹40**. Every answer to this question must lie between ₹40 and ₹66.67, which catches an arithmetic slip immediately.
official_questions.conclusion: EPS ₹6; price ₹45.33 at 20% retention; a retention ratio of 75% (dividend ₹1.50) gives ₹60; and under Gordon the optimum payout is zero because r exceeds Ke.

official_questions.question: Following details are related to H Ltd.: EPS ₹3.00; return on investment 20%; cost of equity 15%. As per Walter's Model, what would be the maximum and minimum price of the share? (2 Marks)
answer_points: ==**Read the question as a question about the optimum payout, not about arithmetic.** Here **r of 20% exceeds Ke of 15%**, so the correlation between dividend and price is **negative**: **the price is highest at a payout of zero and lowest at a payout of 100%**.==

==**The general result worth carrying.** Whenever **r > Ke**: the maximum price is **(r ÷ Ke) × E ÷ Ke** = rE ÷ Ke², and the minimum is simply **E ÷ Ke**. Where **r < Ke** the two swap over. ==So 'maximum and minimum price' never needs more than two substitutions — the endpoints of the payout range.==

**Why the question is only two marks.** There is no EPS working to do, no preference dividend and no reverse solving; the entire content is knowing **which end of the payout range gives which price**. ==A candidate who computes both and labels them the wrong way round scores nothing, which is the whole risk here.==
**Sanity check.** The ratio of the two prices is r ÷ Ke = 20 ÷ 15 = 1.3333, and ₹26.67 ÷ ₹20 = 1.3333. ==That relationship holds in every Walter question, so it is a one-second check on the pair.==
official_questions.conclusion: Maximum ₹26.67 at a nil payout and minimum ₹20 at a 100% payout — because with r above Ke the price falls as the payout rises.
